items.heading: You Cannot Get Years
items.text: You cannot get years of work experience without a job, and you cannot get a job that demands years of experience. That is the catch-22 everyone hits. It breaks in two places at once: widen your definition of what counts as proof of ability, and change where you are aiming your applications.

items.heading: "Entry
items.text: "Entry-level" roles asking for prior experience is not a new complaint, and it is not evidence that you are doing something wrong. It is a structural filter: experience requirements are a cheap, fast way for a recruiter to reduce a large applicant pool, even when the requirement is not strictly necessary for the role. That filter hits two different groups the same way.

items.heading: Before You Can Write Around
items.text: Before you can write around the gap, you need an honest inventory of what you actually have. Most people underestimate this list because they are picturing a formal job offer letter as the only valid unit of experience. It is not.

A generic objective line ("Seeking an opportunity to grow and learn")
A specific line naming the exact skill and the exact evidence for it ("Built three data-cleaning workflows in Excel and Python during coursework; looking to apply this to a junior analyst role")
Apologising for the gap in a cover letter ("I know I lack experience, but")
Naming the transferable mechanism directly ("Three years managing customer complaints as a retail supervisor built the same conflict-resolution and escalation judgment this operations role needs")

items.heading: If a "Trial Project"
items.text: If a "trial project" or "unpaid internship" has no end date, no defined deliverable, and no path to a paid role or a usable proof asset, it has stopped being a tactic and become open-ended free labour. Walk away.

items.heading: The Goal Is a Bounded,
items.text: The goal is a bounded, two-to-five-hour piece of proof, or a short, defined trial with a clear finish line, not a standing arrangement that never converts.
